content: A stye, also referred to as a hordeolum, is a localized and painful infection of the sebaceous glands located at the base of the eyelashes. This infection can occur on the outer surface of the eyelid, inside the eyelid, or beneath it. The condition may resolve spontaneously without medical intervention, but in some cases, the inflammation can spread to other ocular glands or recur. The primary causative agent of a stye is Staphylococcus aureus. Factors such as stress, inadequate nutrition, or insufficient sleep can act as triggers. Additionally, a stye may develop as a secondary complication of blepharitis, a chronic inflammatory condition of the eyelid margins. It is important to distinguish a stye from other conditions that may present similarly, such as xanthelasma, papilloma, cysts, pyogenic granuloma, or amyloid deposition. Certain risk factors increase the likelihood of developing a stye. These include having dry eyes or a history of chronic blepharitis. Styes are particularly prevalent in infants, although they can occur at any age. The initial symptoms of a stye include tenderness and redness in the affected area. Other symptoms may include noticeable swelling, excessive tearing or watering of the eye, sensitivity to light, and discomfort during blinking. On physical examination, a localized, tender area with a small, pointed eruption may be observed. In some cases, a yellowish bump may be visible. Additionally, nearby lymph nodes may be palpable due to the localized infection. In most cases, a stye resolves without the need for medical treatment. Supportive care, such as the application of warm compresses, is often sufficient. Antimicrobial ophthalmic ointments may be used in certain cases, depending on the severity and recurrence of the condition. For a single external hordeolum, warm compresses applied 4-6 times per day are typically adequate. Antibiotic therapy is generally not necessary for a single lesion. However, for multiple or recurrent external hordeola, topical antibiotics such as bacitracin (applied every 8-24 hours) or erythromycin (applied every 4-6 hours) may be prescribed. In cases of internal hordeolum, warm compresses should also be applied 4-6 times daily. Systemic antistaphylococcal antibiotics may be required in conjunction with this therapy.
